questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: For what natural numbers $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the inequality ${2}^{n} > n + 1$& is valid?
questions.solution:
Given that, ${2}^{n} > n + 1$

For $n = 1$, ${2}^{1} > 1 + 1 ⇒ 2 > 2$ is not true

For $n = 2$, ${2}^{2} > 2 + 1 ⇒ 4 > 3$ is True.

So, Given inequality is true for $n = 2$.

Assume that ${2}^{m} > m + 1$ is true for $m > 2$.

But ${2}^{m} > 1$ for all $m > 1$

$⇒ {2}^{m} + {2}^{m} > m + 1 + 1$

$⇒ {2}^{m + 1} > \left(m + 1\right) + 1$

Hence, the inequality holds for $n = m + 1$

It follows by mathematical induction that the given inequality holds for all natural numbers $n \ge 2$.

\(P(m)=2+2^2+2^3+\ldots.+2^m=2^{m+1}\)
So,
\begin{aligned} P(m+1) & =2+2^2+2^3+\ldots.+2^m+2^{m+1} \\
& $=\left(2+2^2+2^3+\ldots.+2^m\right)+2^{m+1} \\
& =2^{(m+1)}+2^{m+1}=2.2^{m+1}=2^{m+2}
\end{aligned}\)
Clearly, if \(P(m)\) is true then \(p(m+1)\) is also true.
\(\therefore P(m)\) is true \(\Rightarrow P(m+1)\) is true.$

$a_0=1, a_{n+1}=3 n^2+n+a_n,(n \geq 0).$
Then, $a_n$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
& \text{ Given, } a_0=1, a_{n+1}=3 n^2+n+a_n \\
& \Rightarrow \quad a_1=3(0)+0+a_0=1 \\
& \text{$ and $} \quad a_2=3(1)^2+1+a_1=3+1+1=5
\end{aligned}$
From option (b),
$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{ Let } & P(n)=n^3-n^2+1 \\
\therefore & P(0)=0-0+1=1=a_0 \\
\text{$ and $} & P(1)=1^3-1^2+1=1=a_1 \\
& P(2)=(2)^3-(2)^2+1=5=a_2
\end{array}$
Hence, option (b) is correct.
